fbn.54: Welcome to the Pelican Town financial market
fbn.56: Carrot Company released its quarterly report this morning: fast growth, high interest rates, the 'first pot of gold' for spring farmers. The CEO stated: 'We don't make the most expensive seeds, just the accounts where you see interest fastest.' — Analysts warn: get in and out fast; don't wait until summer to remember carrots.
fbn.57: Carrot Company's deposit rate reaches 16.67%, but fuel demand isn't low either. Mayor Lewis comments: 'Growing carrots is like quick money — feels great, but don't expect it to support you for life.'
fbn.59: Strawberry Company's spokesperson appeared in a pink suit: 'Though our interest rate was cut in half, we still stand at the top of spring. Sweet, but not cheap.' — From the audience, Abigail whispers: 'Strawberries are indeed sweet, but I don't like discounts.'
fbn.60: Strawberry Company reminds farmers: in continuous harvest mode, don't just focus on single yields. 'Growing a season of strawberries is like a fixed-term deposit. Don't withdraw early, unless you want your interest to turn green.'
fbn.62: Parsnip Company released a statement: 'We don't discount because we're basic enough.' — Bud comments: 'True, even the interest rate can't be bothered to move.' Marnie passes by: 'But the piggies love parsnips.'
fbn.63: Parsnip Company's interest rate is stable at 18.75%, suitable for farmers who don't want complications. Pierre says: 'This is an entry-level financial product, just like my entry-level seeds.'
fbn.65: Green Bean Company's CEO stood on a trellis for the interview: 'We grow tall, and our interest rate stays steady. 17.46% with no discounts — that's the charm of vertical growth.' — Clint: 'I like vertical things.' The moment was briefly awkward.
fbn.66: Green Bean Company emphasizes: 'Continuous harvest, not harvesting interest continuously.' — Analysts: 'But if you don't ship, they do stop growing.'
fbn.68: Potato Company released a yield coefficient correction report today: 'Average 1.2x yield — not luck, but science.' — Bud: 'Scientifically earn more potatoes, and scientifically pay back more loans.'
fbn.69: Potato Company's interest rate is 15.33%, with low fuel demand. Pam comments: 'Potatoes are reliable, unlike certain fruits that cost a fortune and still drop in price.'
fbn.71: Garlic Company: 'Our interest rate is 12.5% — not sexy enough, but it repels vampire-like inflation.' — Sebastian: 'That metaphor is so old-fashioned. But garlic really is useful.'
fbn.72: Garlic Company's final spring shipment reminder: 'Don't wait until summer to remember us. Interest rates don't sprout.'
fbn.74: Unmilled Rice Company issued no comment today. Because their interest rate is negative. Bud: 'This is the only company in Pelican Town where depositing money actually loses you money. My advice: don't deposit — just grow something else.'
fbn.75: Unmilled Rice Company's spokesperson finally spoke up: 'We... we're still refining our product.' George: 'Refining rice? You should be refining your interest rate.'

fbn.78: Cauliflower Company reminds farmers: 'Don't do stupid things just because we look like a brain. Like putting all your deposits with us.'
fbn.80: Kale Company: 'Healthy, stable, no discounts.' — Leah: 'Like my salads. And like my savings account.'

dialogue.3: All debts have been paid off — the townspeople are proud of you!
dialogue.27: I heard you've been a bit tight on cash lately. You know, the grocery store's accounts have always been kept spotless. I hope yours are too.
dialogue.28: Debt — who hasn't dealt with it? But ignoring it only lets the interest snowball. Need to buy seeds? I might be able to convince myself to give you a 5% discount. I said might — no promises.
dialogue.29: You're my best customer and the hardest-working farmer I've ever seen. A little debt is nothing. If you need time to get back on your feet, my counter is always open to you — get those seeds planted first, worry about payment later.
dialogue.30: Pierre sometimes mutters about your financial situation. I don't like talking about people behind their backs, so I'll stop there.
dialogue.31: When I'm tending tea in the greenhouse, I often think: plants don't borrow money, they just grow quietly. Maybe we could learn something from them. Of course, I'm not saying don't borrow. Just... learn to repay quietly.
dialogue.32: Dear, don't let those numbers crush you. I've been married to Pierre for so many years and have seen plenty of ups and downs in the books. Come have some tea — no interest charged.
dialogue.33: As mayor, I must remind you: good credit is the foundation for a farmer to thrive in Pelican Town. I hope you'll sort out your personal finances as soon as possible.
dialogue.34: I've seen Pelican Town weather through storms and high waves. A bad harvest, a messy account — these are all temporary. The town hall isn't here to pressure you about debt. I'm only mentioning it out of concern for you.
dialogue.35: In public I have to stay neutral. But privately, let me tell you: when I was young, I struggled with loans too. There were no dynamic companies back then. Hang in there — Pelican Town needs farmers like you.
dialogue.36: When my pigs owe me feed money, they hide from me too. But at least they grunt an apology. You walk right past my ranch without a grunt.
dialogue.37: Animals have hard times too: cows won't give milk when they're unhappy, chickens won't lay eggs when they're scared. You can't say they 'owe' you. You're the same during tough times. Just... pay it back when you can.
dialogue.38: Dear, I've seen animals survive the coldest winters. What you owe right now is nothing compared to a harsh winter. Need eggs? The kind you don't have to pay back.
dialogue.39: Deadlines wait for no one, and neither do prices. My building contracts have always been hammer-fall pricing. I hope you take that same attitude with the bank.
dialogue.40: I've built enough houses to know what 'unstable foundations' look like. Debt is like your financial foundation sinking. Reinforce it early, or rebuilding later will cost more. That's free financial advice from a carpenter.
dialogue.41: Demetrius once messed up an investment too. It took us a whole year to pay it off. Sebastian was little back then, and Maru had just been born. You're in a much better position than we were. Hang in there.
dialogue.42: At my age, nothing bothers me more than people who borrow money and don't pay it back. In my day, credit was everything. Sigh, you young people these days.
dialogue.43: My legs have been causing me pain for decades. Sometimes it keeps me awake at night. But I understand the pain of debt too. Neither is easy to bear. At least yours can be repaid.
dialogue.44: Come here, child. Let me tell you something: I was in debt once too. Not farming debt — hospital debt. But we paid it off. Everyone falls, but the people of Pelican Town know how to get back up. Evelyn, bring that box of cookies over here for them.
dialogue.45: May Yoba bless you through this hardship. But it's not just about praying — you need to actually pay back the money.
dialogue.46: I baked you some cookies. They won't help pay off your debt, but at least they'll give you something sweet to chew on while you worry. Don't refuse — no interest on cookies.
dialogue.47: Dear child, I see you working hard in your fields every day. George says you're unreliable — I told him to keep his mouth shut. You just need a little time. I have some savings tucked away, but George doesn't know about them. Maybe I could slip you a little. Just maybe.
dialogue.48: I've run this bar long enough to see too many people drown their sorrows in drink. Usually they first owe money elsewhere before they end up owing me for drinks. I hope you're not one of them.
dialogue.49: If you're in debt, don't try to solve it with drinking. Having a drink here is fine, but wrapping your debt notice in tinfoil and drinking over it makes any drink taste bitter. That's Gus's philosophy.
dialogue.50: Kid, I've got an unwritten rule at my bar: regulars going through hard times get the first round on the house. It's not to encourage deadbeats — it's to let you catch your breath. That's all I can do. Coffee or beer?
dialogue.51: You're in debt too? Well, we have something in common then. But don't expect me to bail you out — I'm practically drowning in Joja Cola debt myself.
dialogue.52: Being in debt is actually pretty common. I've owed money, my ex-husband owed money, our whole trailer owed money. But you're different — you can pay it back. I'm not quite so fortunate. So don't end up like me.
dialogue.53: Listen, from someone who's been there: interest snowballs like an avalanche. Don't think you can hold it back. I couldn't hold it back back then, and I'm still buried under it. If you can pay back anything now, do it right away. Aunt Pam's life advice. Take it or leave it.
dialogue.54: In debt? Anxious? Want to run away? Way too familiar. But I'm not your therapist. No advice. Good luck, I guess.
dialogue.55: Want to work at Joja Mart? Never mind, the wages there wouldn't even cover the interest. Forget I said anything. But at least, don't carry it alone.
dialogue.56: I used to think only people like me mess things up. Now seeing someone as hardworking as you also in debt feels... complicated. A little schadenfreude, a little sadness, but mostly — maybe debt isn't entirely a personal failing. Marnie's chickens have been laying well lately. I'll ask her to bring you a box.
dialogue.57: Art requires investment, but not loans. The most important thing I've learned in Pelican Town is this: creativity can help you survive, but don't use it as collateral.
dialogue.58: Sometimes I think money and paint are alike — both can make the world more beautiful, but used wrong, they dirty the canvas. Your canvas just needs a temporary cleaning. Don't rush to sign it away.
dialogue.59: When I lived in the city, I owed money for rent too. It was a lonely feeling. But you're not alone here. If you need a quiet place, come to my cottage. I'll paint, you just sit — no need to say a word.
dialogue.60: A writer's life isn't easy either. Rejected manuscripts, delayed payments, editors' nagging letters piling up. In a sense, we're all debtors. But my collateral is dignity — what's yours?
dialogue.61: Debt is like the villain in a novel. Written well, readers will hate it. Written even better, readers will understand it. But you have to control your pen — don't let the villain take over the story.
dialogue.62: My friend, I once suffered greatly from being unable to write a single word. The pain of debt is probably the same — it devours your attention. But this too shall pass. When you pay off your last gold coin, that novel of yours must be incredible. First signed copy is for me.
dialogue.63: As your doctor, I must point out: financial stress can cause insomnia, anxiety, and digestive problems. Your health is also a health account — don't overdraw it twice.
dialogue.64: Everyone has a limited allowance for anxiety. Yours is completely used up by debt right now, leaving little room to worry about your body. Get regular checkups, even while in debt. I'll delay your medical bills. Not because you're a friend — because you have a doctor.
dialogue.65: You're a strong person. I've seen you come out of the mines covered in wounds and water your crops the next day. That kind of determination can't be defeated by a few loans. Come see me anytime you have health issues — I can't help with money, but I won't let medical bills add to your burden.
dialogue.66: Everyone owing everyone — so boring. Staying in my room was probably the right call. The keyboard doesn't ask me for money. For now.
dialogue.67: I saved all my money. Not because I'm smart — because I'm lazy. The lazy strategy works surprisingly well in times like these. Maybe laziness isn't a flaw — it's risk aversion.
dialogue.68: Hey. You're stressed out, huh? I used to think I was the only 'hide away from everything' type. But you don't seem like the hiding kind. I respect that. If you want to fall apart for one night, I've got games and snacks here.
dialogue.69: My parents always said borrowing money is bad. You owe money? Uh, so they were right?
dialogue.70: If I were you, I'd go beat up slimes in the mines to blow off steam. Wait, you could get hurt and then have to pay medical bills. That'd be worse. Go adventuring instead. Adventuring is free.
dialogue.71: Life was never easy for weird outsiders like us. Other people's rules never seem to fit us. Owning money is just a side effect of you breaking through the rules. I believe you can break every rule, including this one.
dialogue.72: What's it like owing money? Sounds like a hassle. My allowance ran out last week, but at least I don't owe anyone.
dialogue.73: I owed the music store money once too. My dad was furious. But I paid it back eventually — with my gig earnings. Your 'gig' is farming, right? When you pay it off, I'll write a song to commemorate it.
dialogue.74: Dude, Sebastian told me you might be stressed out. But I can't tell. I still think you're cool. Want to come jam at the bar in a few days? Not to drag you into drinking — just to give you a song's worth of time where you don't have to think about all that stuff.
dialogue.75: Based on my compound interest calculations, you should repay as soon as possible. This is a mathematical conclusion, not a social commentary.
dialogue.76: I designed a small program to simulate how interest rate fluctuations affect farm profits and losses. Input your data, and I can tell you the latest safe deadline to pay off. But I won't help you drag it to the last day — that's not safe.
dialogue.77: When you helped me clear slimes from the mines, you said 'no need to thank me.' Now I need to return those words to you. What you owe isn't our goodwill and trust — it's the bank's money. The latter has numbers, the former can't be calculated. So don't stress.
dialogue.78: Thirty years of smithing, not once has anyone bought on credit. You come for a hoe, you bring money. What, you say ore payment terms are negotiable? That's a different story.
dialogue.79: Smelting requires patience. Ore doesn't owe you. You don't owe ore. But money is different. Money is impatient. I had a customer who owed for years before paying it off — now he's my most valued patron. Not because he's rich — because after paying off his debt, he still comes to me for tools.
dialogue.80: I've never had much confidence. But when it comes to owing money, mindset is crucial. If you feel terrible about yourself right now, remember — that's the bank's logic, not the land's. Your tools are just as sharp as ever. I'll sharpen them for you, no labor charge.
dialogue.81: Fish in the sea don't owe each other. But the people on land invented 'borrowing.' Fish are smarter.
dialogue.82: I drifted at sea for a long time before saving enough to open my shop. Never saw a bank while I was drifting. Came back and found they were still there. When you come ashore, the bank will always be there waiting. No rush. Navigate your voyage well.
dialogue.83: Hemingway said a man can be destroyed but not defeated. That's not the exact quote, but close enough. You're not defeated right now — you're just in a storm. I've seen you fishing in the river. You're more patient than any fish. This debt is just a big catch.
dialogue.84: I've observed a disturbance in your energy field. Money itself is a lower-order energy interference, but it attracts more negative presences. Paying off your debt is also cleansing your energy field.
dialogue.85: If you need a quick way to earn money, I know some energy nodes in the forest that can accelerate crop growth. But my advice is: face your predicament calmly. Magic won't pay your debts for you.
dialogue.86: I once owed debts far heavier than gold coins. The dark forces remember every unsettled account. You're still safe. Your debt is just an ordinary obligation. If one day you need to fight greater shadows, come find me. As for the bank's shadow, you can dispel that yourself.
dialogue.87: Humans always talk about money. Shadows don't need money. So shadows are better.
dialogue.88: I've lived here a long time. Seen many humans. Humans in debt are the most anxious. Anxious humans do stupid things. You must be careful — don't do stupid things. Krobus can sell you Void Eggs. Not for free. But cheaper than the bank.
dialogue.89: You're the only human I trust. I have nothing to help you repay with, but I can tell you a secret — deep in the Skull Cavern, treasure is hidden. I can't tell you where. But if you go, remember to come back and visit me. Not to repay me — I'll miss you.
dialogue.90: My kind keeps grudges, not accounts. Not paying back money? That's nothing. Owning a head — that's a grudge.
dialogue.91: In dwarven mines, ore belongs to the finder. The concept of debt was invented by humans. We only recognize plunder and loss. If you're willing to think of your debt as 'lost ore,' I can keep an eye out for you in the mines.
dialogue.92: Human laws are beyond me. Your 'interest' is like a weak dwarf — it only clings to the strong and gets fat off them. You're strong — you proved that in the mines. Shake it off.
dialogue.93: From a scientific perspective, debt is a negative asset state. It makes your decision-making model irrational. I suggest you eliminate this variable as soon as possible.
dialogue.94: I've studied local crop growth cycles and market price fluctuations. If you need to optimize your planting strategy to accelerate returns, I can provide some data support. But data is just data — the hoe is in your hands.
dialogue.95: Robin told me about what her family went through back then. As a scientist, I shouldn't have just shown her data reports — I should have given her a hug first. I understand your current situation. If you need my lab to help analyze soil or fertilizer efficiency, come by anytime. No consulting fee.
dialogue.96: I teach children what 'credit' means in class. I hope you can be a good example for them. Take care of your situation soon, alright?
dialogue.97: Education is a long-term investment, sometimes with no visible returns. Your farm is the same. Don't let your current debt negate all your past efforts. The children are still waiting for you to come tell farm stories at school next time.
dialogue.98: My mother struggled with debt her whole life. I know what that feels like. So don't worry — I won't bore you with lectures. If you need a quiet place to read and forget about those numbers for a while, there's always room in my little library. Jas and Vincent like you — don't let them see you looking so sad.
dialogue.99: Teacher Penny says borrowing money is bad. Did you not do your math homework properly?
dialogue.100: Do you need money? I saved two coins. Mommy said I can give coins to people who need them. Do you need them? No need to pay back.
dialogue.101: I don't really understand what debt is. But I think you're a good person. Good people shouldn't be sad. Do you want to see my drawing? I drew your farm with lots and lots of pumpkins — more than the numbers in the bank.
dialogue.102: Will you go to jail for owing money? Sam says no. I hope Sam is right.
dialogue.103: Daddy says you have to pay back what you owe, but he didn't say what to do if you can't. Maybe you can come eat at our house. Eating doesn't create debt. Mommy said so.
dialogue.104: You're the coolest farmer! Can even the coolest farmer owe money? Then maybe owing money isn't so bad. When I grow up, I'm going to invent something that doesn't cost any money, and you'll be the first to use it.
dialogue.105: The rule of the desert: water is worth more than gold. What are you short on right now — water or gold? If it's gold, I can't help. If it's water, come in for a cup of cactus tea.
dialogue.106: Oh dear, I've seen countless travelers at the Oasis. Some come with pockets full of gold, some come weighed down by debt. But the desert doesn't care. The sun rises as usual. Your farm will too.
dialogue.107: I'll tell you a secret — I have a few old clients in the city who deal in premium flowers. If they saw your flowers, they'd probably be fighting over them. Next time you come, I'll give you their contact info. Not to help you — I want them to see what real flowers look like. Helping you is just a side effect.
dialogue.108: The Adventurer's Guild doesn't handle financial disputes. We handle lives. But if you're too afraid to enter the mines because of debt, we'll have to consider whether you can still be a member.
dialogue.109: Monsters won't go easy on you because you owe money. Don't bring your anxiety into the mines. Focus on saving your life, not your accounts. Going down and coming back alive is worth more than any interest rate.
dialogue.110: I've prepared a set of backup equipment for you. It's not a freebie — if you truly reach the end of your rope, come find me. Some guild members have owed me things before. I help out, but not often. You're a special case.
dialogue.111: I visit farms across the region year-round. Poor financial health is a precursor to farm decline. I don't want Pelican Town adding 'former farmer' after your name. That would have a big impact on the local economy.
dialogue.112: Agricultural lending policy winds do shift. I can't promise anything, but when the next council discussion comes around, your situation will be among the cases I consider.
dialogue.113: When I was young, I farmed in the countryside too and owed what seemed like an unpayable sum at the time. I paid it off and became governor. So don't write yourself off before you've paid it back. At the Pelican Town Cranberry Festival, I want to see you still at your booth.
dialogue.114: The town hall understands your situation. Pelican Town's agricultural system has a responsibility to provide a safety net for farmers. But this net can only catch the bottom — it can't pull you out. You'll have to climb out yourself.
dialogue.115: Speaking as your mayor, and also as your friend: bankruptcy is not the end. I've arranged for the town hall to prepare a small emergency relief fund for you. It's not much, but at least it'll help you get through the next few days. Pelican Town doesn't abandon its own farmers.
dialogue.116: Listen, I know going through official channels in public is too slow. This money is mine personally. Not the town's, not the taxpayers' — mine. Take it. When your farm recovers, just ship a little extra to the town later. Don't tell anyone. It's not because I'm embarrassed — it's because this isn't proper procedure. But I'm your friend first, mayor second.
dialogue.117: The animals' winters are harsher than ours, but they always survive. You can too.
dialogue.118: I had the pigs till an extra patch of land for you. Of course, they root around everywhere anyway. But this time was for you. Bankruptcy is nothing — your pockets were even emptier when you first arrived.
dialogue.119: Dear, take these eggs. I know you probably can't even afford seeds right now. An animal's gift is different from the bank's — they don't need you to pay it back. When you get back on your feet, just come see them. I only found out about your situation because Lewis came by specifically to ask about reducing your rent. Thanks to him (laughs).
dialogue.120: Buildings collapse, farms go bankrupt, but the foundation remains. Your foundation is this land, not those numbers.
dialogue.121: If you need to expand or renovate your farm to start over, I can delay the charges. Not free — I trust you'll earn it back. A carpenter's trust is worth more than a bank's credit.
dialogue.122: I told you before that my family went through hard times too. That wasn't just being polite. Take this lumber. It's nothing valuable, but enough to fix a few fences or build a small barrel. Don't feel alone during the rebuilding — we went through that phase too.
dialogue.123: Bankruptcy is certainly tricky. But you're still an important customer at the grocery store. Don't lose heart. Just keep coming in to shop.
dialogue.124: I almost went bankrupt when I was starting out too. Your situation is not unique. As long as your land is still there, you can stand back up. The grocery store counter will always be saved for you.
dialogue.125: Take these seeds. It's not an expensive gift, but I picked out mixed seeds that grow in every season. I don't know what you can plant right now, but at least you'll have something to sow into the ground. When your hands are holding seeds, bankruptcy doesn't count.
dialogue.126: There's an old saying at sea: the ship sinks, but as long as the sailor lives, it's not a failure. Your ship sank — not you.
dialogue.127: I've experienced worse than bankruptcy at sea. That ship is still at the bottom of the ocean, but I'm here. You'll be here too.
dialogue.128: Take this bait. Don't rush to rebuild the farm. Go fishing first. Clear your head. When you catch the Legend, you'll know you've still got it.
dialogue.129: After bankruptcy, you need to eat well even more. Not luxuriously — just properly. The Stardrop Saloon welcomes you.
dialogue.130: Before I opened this bar, I was a chef working for someone else. People said I couldn't make it either. But look at me now — standing in my own bar. Your farm is still there, and you can stand on your own land too.
dialogue.131: This salad is today's special. Try it. I know you still have income, but a free meal is a restaurant owner's kindness to a friend. Not charity. It's not on the menu, and I'll never charge you for it.
dialogue.132: On the loom of fate, some threads always break. When they break, rethread them. Your thread is still there.
dialogue.133: During meditation, I saw your aura — it's green. Even though you feel terrible right now, your aura tells me: you will grow back.
dialogue.134: This is handwoven by me. For you. Not to sell for money — put it by your pillow. Touch it every morning when you wake up to remind yourself — someone still believes in you.
dialogue.135: Bankruptcy sounds so terrible. You'll be okay, right? I need you to say yes. Just say yes.
dialogue.136: People in fashion go bankrupt and still keep wearing haute couture. You're no worse than them. At least you still have a good pair of shoes for working the fields. Don't hang your head.
dialogue.137: This is my favorite flower. It always faces the sun. You might be in the shadows right now, but don't turn your face away.
dialogue.138: Art history is full of creators who lived in poverty. You're not impoverished — you just don't have liquid assets temporarily.
dialogue.139: I once started painting from a pile of ruins. You just have an extra number on your farm ledger. That's no ruin. Don't dramatize it.
dialogue.140: This salad is made from vegetables I grew myself. You taught me how. Now I'm giving back to you with your own method.
dialogue.141: I'm way too familiar with the feeling of bankruptcy. I'm on the edge of it every day. But it hasn't killed me, and it won't kill you.
dialogue.142: Hey. If you start drinking too much because of bankruptcy, come to me first. I'll have a round with you, and then we'll go recover together the next day. At least you won't be alone.
dialogue.143: With this bottle, I won't say 'don't drink too much.' I'll say — while drinking, think of it as a celebration. Celebrating that you didn't fall.
dialogue.144: What's the first thing you want to do after bankruptcy? Run away. I know. But don't follow my example.
dialogue.145: When I hit rock bottom, Marnie caught me. You've fallen now, but I won't catch you — you don't need me to. Your account is bankrupt, not your heart.
dialogue.146: This pizza is from Joja Mart. I know you don't like Joja, and I don't like myself either. But eat up, then get back to work.
dialogue.147: Your health account isn't bankrupt yet. When you come back for a checkup, I'll charge you as usual, because by then you'll definitely have bounced back.
dialogue.148: Stress is related to cortisol levels. Bankruptcy can max out your stress, but it won't blow out your heart. You're very strong — it says so right in your medical report.
dialogue.149: Vitamins. Not for paying off debts — for getting through the season. A healthy body keeps a clear mind. This is a doctor's prescription — no bill attached.
dialogue.150: Statistically, temporary bankruptcy is a form of financial restructuring. Rational analysis shows you still have a chance.
dialogue.151: I ran a simulation for you. If you start growing Parsnips from scratch, you should recover your basic cash flow in about one season. Not too hard.
dialogue.152: This battery is charged with my lab's strongest current. I'm giving it to you so you know — the energy is still there. Your farm needs to recharge too.
dialogue.153: Hiding after bankruptcy is perfectly normal. I stayed in my room for three years — that was a kind of bankruptcy too. A social bankruptcy.
dialogue.154: If you want to escape from everyone, I'll lend you my basement. Come at night, leave in the morning. Nobody will see. You don't need to explain.
dialogue.155: These things aren't worth much. But they fell out of the darkness. While you're walking through the dark, pick them up on the way.
dialogue.156: Bankruptcy is like a boss fight in a game. You think you can't win, but really you just need more levels. Just level up.
dialogue.157: I'll go adventuring with you. Not real adventuring — just beating up slimes in the mines. They won't fight back. Great stress relief.
dialogue.158: The amethyst can protect you. Just kidding, I don't know if it can. But I think it puts my mind at ease, and lets you know I want to protect you.
dialogue.159: Bankruptcy is tragic, my friend. Truly. But I wrote a song.
dialogue.160: The song is called 'When Gold Coins No Longer Jingle.' The melody is decent, but the lyrics are... I'd better not sing it for you here. Listen when you're back on your feet.
dialogue.161: This was the snack that made me happiest as a kid. I didn't save any money to help you, but I saved some maple candy. Here. Don't turn your nose up at it.
dialogue.162: Tragedy is the highest form of literature. You're living out a tragedy right now. But the protagonist of every tragedy ultimately finds awakening.
dialogue.163: I'll write a poem for you. Whether it gets published or not doesn't matter. What matters is that you became my inspiration. Not mockery — a tribute.
dialogue.164: This quill is from my writing desk. I touch it every time writing gets hard. Now it's yours. When your bankruptcy becomes a story too, you'll need a prop.
dialogue.165: I've never gone bankrupt, but I ended up in a wheelchair. I've lost more than money. You're luckier than me.
dialogue.166: Evelyn told me to speak gently to you. So here it is, gently: Stand up. Not your legs — you, as a person.
dialogue.167: These stones are from my collection when I was young. Useless, but hard. Like you. Keep them. Throw them around for fun if you want.
dialogue.168: May Yoba bless you. In your darkest hour, light will shine in from the most unexpected place.
dialogue.169: George is tough-mouthed, but last night he asked how you were doing. He never asks about other people. Your roots in Pelican Town run deeper than you think.
dialogue.170: Fresh out of the oven. Eat it while it's hot. If it's not enough, there's more. Yoba taught me: feeding a person is feeding a future. Your future is sweet.
dialogue.171: Iron bends but doesn't break. You're the same. My iron never lies to me, and I won't lie to you.
dialogue.172: You're the hardest-working farmer I've ever seen. I don't hand out that compliment often. You just got bitten by numbers. Let me see your wounds — no, I mean go show the doctor. I'm just a blacksmith.
dialogue.173: Iron. Not worth much money, but worth a heartfelt gesture. Take it and make tools. Smash something else, or hammer out a new beginning.
dialogue.174: Bankruptcy is a state of being, not a curse. Your destiny is still in your own hands.
dialogue.175: I've observed your horoscope — Pluto is in retrograde, and that's not your fault. The universe occasionally bankrupts mortals to teach them humility. You're not someone who needs humility, so this seems unfair. But the universe doesn't care. You need to.
dialogue.176: This geode has the ability to absorb negative energy. Bury it on your farm, and a little luck will grow in spring. I can't promise that. But I can promise you're already lucky enough — so many people are standing by your side.
dialogue.177: Bankruptcy protection is an institutional design meant to buy you time for restructuring. Please use that time wisely.
dialogue.178: I've observed your work on the farm. Your energy output efficiency ranks among the best in Pelican Town. This temporary downturn won't change your baseline rate. Just keep going.
dialogue.179: This is my own custom-blended Deluxe Fertilizer. Not charity — it's a test sample. Help me test how it performs in poor soil conditions. Robin says you don't need a reason to give things, but I made one up anyway.
dialogue.180: The children ask about you, and I tell them you're going through a hard time. They don't press further. Children understand 'everything will be all right' better than adults do.
dialogue.181: I teach in town on a meager salary. I can't help you with much money, but I can bring you a bouquet of wildflowers and leave them at your door. Not a gift — a reminder that as long as there are flowers on the windowsill, life isn't so bad.
dialogue.182: This book is called 'Seeds and Patience.' It's my favorite picture book. Jas can already read it, and she wants to lend it to you. She said, 'Farmer brother/sister needs stories the most right now.' Kid logic. But I agreed.
dialogue.183: Are you bankrupt? Mommy says bankruptcy means money disappears. Sometimes I lose my allowance too. So we're the same.
dialogue.184: Vincent and I talked about it. We have a secret clubhouse, and we can share a small part of it with you. You won't need to spend any money inside. There are no banks in the secret clubhouse.
dialogue.185: This is a little clay figure I made. One is you, and one is your cat/dog. They'll never go bankrupt. Together forever.
dialogue.186: Do you not have money for sugar anymore? I'll share half of mine with you. Not lending — sharing.
dialogue.187: Jas said she wants to help you. I want to help too. But all I have are marbles. Can marbles help?
dialogue.188: This sweet thing is from Mommy's kitchen. She said I can give it to friends. You're my friend. Mommy says friends should eat sweet things even more when they go bankrupt.
dialogue.189: Bankruptcy is routine in the desert. Lizards can lose their tails every day they go out. But they grow back. You will too.
dialogue.190: The Oasis shop can put a bottle of Cactus Fruit Wine on credit for you. Not free, but the payment terms can be extended until you're no longer anxious.
dialogue.191: These seeds only grow in the desert, but I know you can grow them on your farm. Rare crops sell at a good price. You don't have to split the profits with me — just give me a pot of it. I like looking at it.
dialogue.192: Bankruptcy and death are two different things. You're still standing here talking to me.
dialogue.193: Monsters in the Shadow Mines drop valuable loot. I'm not encouraging you to risk your life to repay debt. I'm saying — when you hold a weapon, you're not just a debtor. You're a hunter.
dialogue.194: Drink this. Not so you go get yourself killed — so you know this: the Guild can afford this one life. Those debt numbers don't deserve to take yours.
dialogue.195: Bankruptcy protection is your right under the law. I don't judge. But I expect to see your name on Pelican Town's farm output list next year.
dialogue.196: The state government has a small grant program for farm bankruptcy recovery. The paperwork is tedious, but the amount is worth it. I'll have them mail the application to you. Fill it out or not — your choice. That's all I'm at liberty to share.
dialogue.197: In an official capacity, I can't directly provide aid. But this fertilizer is 'agricultural demonstration and extension material.' Extending it to you is within regulations. Use it well.
dialogue.198: Oh, by the way — your account is settled. In the grocery store's ledger, your page is now spotlessly clean. Keep it up.
dialogue.199: Speaking of which, you've paid off everything you owed last time, right? I knew you weren't the type to drag things out. Next time you come to the store, coffee's on me. Not a discount — a celebration.
dialogue.200: I was just flipping through the old ledger, and I saw the page with your debt crossed out. I stared at that line for a good while. You know what? I tore that page out and kept it. The day your farm becomes a Pelican Town legend, that piece of paper will be the beginning of the story.
dialogue.201: By the way — on the town hall's financial records, your debt has been cleared to zero. This is official, so you can breathe a sigh of relief.
dialogue.202: More good news: the town hall just confirmed that all your debts have been fully settled. As your mayor, I'm happy for you. Truly. Not just being polite.
dialogue.203: Actually, I made a special trip to the town hall archives this morning. I pulled out your loan file and stamped it 'Settled.' Stamping that seal was the happiest thing I've done all year.
dialogue.204: I heard you paid off all your money! I knew you could do it.
dialogue.205: Hey. I saw you going through the ledger late last night. I didn't say anything, but I was awake. If you want to talk, I'm here. If you don't, I'm still here. When I married you, I didn't sign any 'only together during good times' clause. But if you stay up late again, I'm confiscating your game controller.
dialogue.206: Dear, after you fell asleep last night, I looked at your ledger. Should I have? But I did. Then I sat in the moonlight for a long time. Not worrying — thinking about how to write this chapter into my novel. You're the most protagonist-like person I've ever met, and every protagonist goes through a low point in the second act. Marrying you means marrying this story. You won't write the ending alone.
dialogue.207: As your doctor: I check your blood pressure weekly, and I'll add an extra check during your debt period. As your husband: I've set aside an emergency fund in my clinic drawer. It's not that I don't trust you to repay it yourself — it's there in case you need to catch your breath. Don't be upset. There's no line item for this in the medical handbook. But it's in the husband's job description.
dialogue.208: You've been changing clothes less often lately. You used to check the mirror three times before heading out — now you just run. I'm not criticizing you for being sloppy — I'm saying, debt is making you forget who you are. You're the most beautiful person I've ever met, and it's not because of the clothes. It's the way you stand in the sunlight. That can't be ruined by numbers.
dialogue.209: I've been going through paint in my studio at an unusual rate. Not making new work — I'm painting you. Every time you stare blankly at the ledger, I paint another one. There's one called 'The Weight of Numbers,' and another called 'But His Hands Are Still in the Soil.' I married a farmer, not an account book. When you've conquered all those numbers, I'm going to hold an exhibition called 'The Winner.' You'll be one of the exhibits.
dialogue.210: I wrote a small program for your ledger that calculates the most optimal repayment order. Not to help you procrastinate — to help you precisely strike at every gold coin's interest. You always say you're not good with numbers, and that's fine. I am. One of the reasons I married you is — you can see things I can't. Now it's my turn to lend you my eyes.
dialogue.211: The children asked me today why you haven't been around much lately. I told them you're fighting a very hard boss — that's the way Abigail taught me to put it. Jas drew a picture for me to bring you — it shows you holding a sword, and on the sword it says 'Patience.' She says this weapon is invincible. Every word I've taught her, she's applied to you. Including 'hero.'
dialogue.212: Hey. I wrote a song. This time it's not one of those sad songs I secretly wrote while you were still in debt. It's a — how should I put it — a 'you've definitely got this' song. The melody's been spinning in my head for two days, but the lyrics aren't finished yet. Because I don't know the ending. When you knock out all those debts, I can write the final verse. My guitar is waiting for your good news.
dialogue.213: Your ledger was on the table. I glanced at it when I walked by. Then I went back to the basement for a while. Not hiding — just thinking. I used to think I owed the world, then I realized the world doesn't care. But you care. You care about what you owe, and you care about me. So this time I'm not hiding. You don't need to hide either. I'll split the basement with you. The keyboard is free, and so is the coffee I make.
dialogue.214: I once owed Joja Mart, owed Marnie favors, owed myself a whole mess of debts. I thought owing money was exclusive to people like me. Turns out you owe money too. You know what I thought? I thought — great, I'm experienced in this area. Not schadenfreude. It's that I can finally not be the one being helped in front of you. Let me be there as you repay it. Not the money — let me help you repay this damn anxiety.
dialogue.215: You're in debt. Shadows don't have money, and don't need money. But you do. I'm confused. What confuses me is -- you've already shown me human light, so why is the light being hidden by numbers? I don't understand debt. But I understand you. If you need to, you can sell more void eggs. Not me selling. You selling. The eggs are mine, the money is yours. This isn't a transaction. It's cohabitation.
dialogue.216: Take it. My amethyst. Before I said it could protect you, and you didn't believe me. Believe it or not, take it now. It's not for selling -- it's for putting under your pillow. We can play games all night tonight, or do nothing at all. Bankruptcy is just a boss in your life. You're not fighting alone. Your teammate is here. Full health, full mana.
dialogue.217: You've seen this feather. I touch it when I'm struggling to write. Now it's yours -- no, it's ours. I have another one on my desk. So every debt you owe is between two feathers. One with you, one with me. In novels, this kind of setup is called a 'token.' A token won't make the debt disappear. But it reminds you the story isn't over. Ours isn't over.
dialogue.218: Vitamins, energy supplements, and a handwritten letter. The letter isn't a prescription, it's a love letter. I checked your medical report for you -- everything is normal except your stress levels are a bit high. Normal means your body is far healthier than your ledger. I married you, not your farm. You went bankrupt, but you didn't. My prescription is just getting started.
dialogue.219: Last time I said sunflowers always face the sun. Now I know -- the sun gets tired too. So you don't always have to be the sun. Today let's switch. You be the flower, I'll be the sun. This isn't charity. It's taking turns on watch. You've been shining on me for so long, it's my turn to shine on you. Here, a sunflower. I still have the first one you gave me. This is the third now.
dialogue.220: Salad. The first dish you taught me. You said, 'A salad made with your own crops, eaten without owing anyone.' Now you're bankrupt, and this saying works in reverse -- the salad I make uses your method, and you eat it without owing me. Because what you taught me is worth more than a meal. I didn't say that, you did back then. I'm just returning it to you.
dialogue.221: Two fully charged batteries. One for your farming tools, one for your bedside lamp. During the day you're in the fields and need energy. At night you're home and need light. I'm a scientist, I can't say romantic things. But I've calculated -- how much energy you've put into this farm, and how much energy you've put into this home. The latter is an order of magnitude greater. Data doesn't lie. And neither does my love for you.
dialogue.222: 'Seeds and Patience.' Last time it was a loan, this time it's a gift. Jas heard you went bankrupt -- she doesn't really understand what bankruptcy means -- she said to give you the book because you 'haven't finished planting.' The child is right. Your farm isn't finished. Your story isn't finished either. What page the bookmark is on doesn't matter. What matters is you haven't closed the book.
dialogue.223: Two maple candy bars. One for you, one for me. You went bankrupt, but you didn't fall. When I was little eating these, I thought the world was wonderful. Now I'm grown and know the world isn't that great. But you make me feel that even if it's not that great, there's still something sweet here. It's not the candy. It's carrying these burdens with you. Eat up. After, I'll play music for you. You can request songs.
dialogue.224: Ten void essences. Dropped from the darkest mines. You always said you could pick things back from the darkness. Now you're in the dark, let me pick them up. I'm not saying you fell in -- I'm saying you're walking through. These essences aren't worth much, but I saved them for a long time. While saving, I didn't think 'in case you need them' -- I thought 'you'll always need them.' I rarely say things like this. But you're not just anyone.
dialogue.225: Pizza and beer. Same as last time -- Joja pizza, the version of me I hate. But not today. Today this beer is a celebration. Celebrating that you didn't fall. Celebrating that you didn't become me. Celebrating that even during bankruptcy you could get up at six in the morning to water the crops. What I couldn't do, you did. You make me think maybe I can do some things too. Eat. I'll eat with you. When you quit drinking, I'll quit with you. You're not alone.
dialogue.226: Five void eggs. Not bought. A gift from your cohabitant. You went bankrupt, and the numbers of the human world say you failed. But there's no failure in the shadows. There's only 'still here' and 'no longer here.' You're still here. I'm here too. So it's not failure. It's just a temporary misunderstanding by human numbers. Put these eggs on the farm. They look beautiful when they float. Beautiful things will make you forget the numbers.
dialogue.228: You did it. I mean, you beat that boss by yourself. Even though I was healing you from the side, you dealt the damage. I didn't tell you -- I drew you staying up late going through your ledgers during your debt period. The painting is called 'Warrior's Intermission.' I won't show you unless you promise not to take such a long intermission again. We can start New Game Plus now.
dialogue.229: I finished the last chapter of the novel. The protagonist paid off his debt. It's not a coincidence -- I was waiting for you. The ending I wrote is: 'He put down his pen. Outside the window, in the fields, that person was harvesting the last batch of crops. He was no longer a debtor. He had always been loved.' After publication, this page will be printed with 'Dedicated to my farmer.' Not for romance. Because it's the truth -- you are my inspiration.
dialogue.230: I filed your last checkup records. The label changed from 'Under Observation' to 'Fully Recovered.' But my private file -- not the clinic's, the one in my heart -- the label says 'My Hero.' You're the best case a doctor husband could ever have, and the best partner too. No need to check blood pressure tonight. I can hear your heartbeat.
dialogue.231: You've started looking in the mirror again. This morning I secretly watched you straighten your collar, and you didn't notice. When I married you, I knew life would be tough -- not that you'd be tough, but that life would be. But you always manage to pull yourself back together. This time you pulled yourself back. Now you can be my sun again. What looks good on me? You decide.
dialogue.232: I've packed up all the paintings from the exhibition. But the last one I want to repaint. Because the original ending had you still in front of the ledger, but now you've stood up. The new painting is called 'After the Sunny Day.' You said you could come pick it up -- now it's about time. Actually, you don't need to pick it up. The person in the painting wasn't painted by me. You painted yourself. I just adjusted the colors.
dialogue.233: Data update. Your liabilities are zero, the soil vitality index is rising, and my simulation model accurately predicted the repayment cycle -- wait, no, you didn't follow the optimal repayment path. You were faster than the model. My model needs to be corrected, adding a variable called 'Spouse's Irrational Perseverance.' I can't quantify it. But I know it kicked in every time you wanted to give up. I'm not publishing the paper. This variable belongs only to you.
dialogue.234: You still have that book. Jas asked about you again in class today. I told her your debt was paid off. She said, 'Then he can return the book to the library.' I said no -- that book has already been given away by you. She said, 'Then give another one.' I said no need, because the story is already in someone. She doesn't understand what that means. But you do. Tonight I'll read you a new story. This time, not about seeds. About harvests.
dialogue.235: The song is done. It's called 'Coins Jingling.' Not 'Coins No Longer Jingling' -- that's the old version. The new version is danceable. You said you can't dance, but last night at the bar, your feet were tapping to the beat. I saw it. Honey, you're the first person I've ever seen who made the coins jingle again. At the next show, this song is the encore. You're sitting in the front row. It's not an invitation -- it's an assignment.
dialogue.236: You walked out of the darkness. I won't claim it was my doing. But I left a light on my desk. Every night before you go back to the bedroom, you pass through the basement. The light was left by me. Did you see it? It's fine if you didn't. It's morning now. I'm going to turn the light off. But let me tell you -- I left the light on for you. This is the most un-Sebastian thing I've ever done. Because of you.
dialogue.237: You paid it off. I watched you pay it off. Every day. Every day you came back from the fields covered in mud. One night I couldn't sleep, so I made a list of every number you owed. Then I stared at that list for a long time. Not because of the numbers -- because behind those numbers was you, hacking away one hoe strike at a time. You turned that list into scrap paper. You didn't break yourself. You broke my excuses. I'm quitting. Not for you. To be worthy of being your husband. But you're the one who made me believe I could.
